soil-water-166.title: How full the pores are: degree of saturation
soil-water-166.text: Fill every pore of a soil with water and its degree of saturation is 1. Empty them all and it is 0. Degree of saturation, a measure used in soil mechanics and petroleum engineering, tells how fully a material's pore space is filled with water. Yet no real material ever reaches either end, so both values are idealizations for engineering. Soil physicists often use effective saturation instead, a dimensionless value defined by van Genuchten and also called normalized water content. It runs between two practical limits. Residual water content is where water content stops changing as suction head rises. Saturated water content equals the {{ref:soil-phys-063}}.

soil-water-192.title: Why coarse sand passes water a million times faster than clay
soil-water-192.text: Coarse sand may let water through over a million times more readily than clay. Allen Hazen found why: a soil's coefficient of permeability rises with the square of its particle size. The permeability of soils is a soil's capacity to let water pass, and grain size is only the start. Permeability also rises with {{ref:soil-phys-073}}. Plot void ratio against the logarithm of k, and every soil gives a straight line. Fine impurities in the water progressively clog the pores. Fine-grained soils carry a strongly attached film of adsorbed water that gravity cannot move, and it obstructs flow. Air pockets in partly saturated soil block water too, so permeability falls well below its saturated value and Darcy's law no longer strictly applies. Entrapped air and organic material both cut permeability considerably, which is why test samples must be fully saturated. In the field, compaction lowers permeability and raises runoff, while vegetative cover raises it.

soil-water-167.title: Weighing a soil's water by baking it out
soil-water-167.text: The most direct way to measure a soil's water is to bake it out. In the oven-dry method, a sample goes into a special oven or kiln and is weighed at regular intervals until drying is complete. The mass lost is the water. Dividing it by the wet or the dry mass, depending on the discipline, gives gravimetric water content. Volumetric water content also needs the sample's total volume, fixed by filling a container of known volume, such as a tin can, when sampling. Because it needs a sample removed, dried and weighed, soil moisture sensors estimate water indirectly instead, from electrical resistance, dielectric constant or neutron interaction.

soil-water-169.title: Reading soil moisture from orbit with microwaves
soil-water-169.text: Clouds that hide the ground from a camera do not stop a microwave. Satellites estimate surface soil moisture with microwaves, using the large contrast in dielectric properties between wet and dry soil. Microwaves are insensitive to atmospheric conditions, pass through clouds and partly penetrate vegetation to read the ground surface. Satellites used this way include WindSat, AMSR-E, RADARSAT, ERS-1-2, Metop/ASCAT and SMAP. They take {{ref:soil-water-168}} off the ground and into orbit.

soil-water-241.title: Bioclogging: when microbes seal the soil's pores
soil-water-241.text: Under water that is never drained away, soil can seal itself. Bioclogging is the blocking of soil pores by microbial cells and their byproducts, such as the slime described in {{ref:soil-bio-080}}. The biomass forms an impermeable layer that sharply cuts {{ref:soil-water-180}}. It typically appears under continuous ponding, in recharge ponds, irrigation channels, sewers and riverbeds. In submerged soil, permeability falls, rises as trapped air dissolves, then falls for 2 to 4 weeks as microbes clog the pores. Methane bubbles from microbes clog pores too. Regular drying and cleaner water reduce it. Sometimes the seal is welcome. It lines dairy wastewater ponds, cuts seepage from irrigation channels inoculated with algae and bacteria, and aids compacted clay landfill liners.

soil-water-154.title: How wet soil steadies the weather
soil-water-154.text: Soil moisture shapes more than a harvest. Water has roughly double the heat capacity of soil, so wetter soil warms and cools more slowly under the same heating. Through the soil's temperature, moisture then affects biological triggers such as seed germination, flowering and the activity of soil fauna. The effect reaches the sky. Climate modelling by Timbal and colleagues in 2002 linked soil moisture to the persistence and variability of surface temperature and rainfall in Australia. Soil water now matters for climate modelling and weather prediction, and the Global Climate Observing System lists it among its 50 Essential Climate Variables.

soil-water-174.title: Salty soil water that roots cannot drink
soil-water-174.text: A soil can be wet and still leave a seedling thirsty. Osmotic potential is the part of {{ref:soil-water-172}} lowered by dissolved solutes. Pure water is set at zero, so it can never be positive. The soil solution carries inorganic and organic solutes, and the more it holds, the lower its osmotic potential. Zones of soil are rarely separated by a semipermeable membrane, so this potential has little effect on how water moves through soil. Plants are another matter. In soils high in soluble salts, the low osmotic potential severely restricts water uptake by roots. It can fall so low that the cells of young seedlings collapse by plasmolysis.

soil-water-202.title: When water rushes too fast for Darcy's law
soil-water-202.text: {{ref:soil-water-201}} assumes that flow keeps step with pressure. Push a fluid fast enough and that breaks down. The Reynolds number compares a flow's inertia with its viscosity, and above values of about 1 to 10, inertial effects become significant. The Forchheimer equation extends Darcy's law with an inertial term, using an inertial permeability measured in metres. The cause lies at the pore scale, where recirculation zones change the shape of the flow streamlines. Flow within a sandstone reservoir is usually too slow to need it. Gas flowing into a production well, or through rough fractures, may justify it.

soil-water-186.title: Sorptivity: how readily a dry material drinks
soil-water-186.text: Soil, brick, stone and concrete all soak up water by capillarity, and sorptivity measures how readily. John Philip introduced the term in 1957 for a porous medium's capacity to absorb or release liquid by {{ref:soil-phys-095}}. In 1969 he showed how to find it from horizontal infiltration, which is mostly capillary absorption. Its SI unit is m·s−1/2. For vertical infiltration, Philip's solution adds a second parameter, giving equations valid for short times. Clapp and Hornberger derived average sorptivity values for different texture classes.

soil-water-227.title: SMAP, NASA's watch on the planet's soil moisture
soil-water-227.text: Every 2 to 3 days, one satellite takes a global snapshot of soil moisture. Soil Moisture Active Passive, or SMAP, is a NASA mission that measures soil moisture and its freeze-thaw state across the planet. It launched on 31 January 2015 with a passive L-band radiometer and an active radar. An amplifier failure ended the radar that same year, and the mission carries on with the radiometer alone. It senses the top 5 cm of soil through moderate vegetation, and hydrologic models extend the readings down to the root zone. That is often enough to catch single storms. The data improve drought monitoring, flood and landslide forecasts, weather prediction and famine early warning.

soil-found-105.title: Throughflow: water slipping sideways under a slope
soil-found-105.text: Not all water that soaks in sinks straight down. Infiltrated water still moves under gravity toward the water table, but where permeability varies sideways it can travel downslope instead. Throughflow is this lateral, unsaturated flow through the soil, typically in a permeable layer lying over a less permeable one. It usually runs during peak events such as heavy rain, at rates set by the {{ref:soil-water-193}} of the medium. The water returns to the surface as return flow before or on entering a stream or groundwater. It carries things with it: bases in the B horizon of a {{ref:soil-class-138}} may be lost this way.

soil-water-242.title: Plinthite, the red clay that sets like stone
soil-water-242.text: In highly weathered soils, a soft red clay can turn to rock in the sun. Plinthite is an iron-rich, humus-poor mixture of clay with quartz and other minerals. It forms in soil horizons saturated with water for part of the year, usually as dark red concretions in platy, polygonal or reticulate patterns. Moist, it cuts with a spade; drier, near {{ref:soil-water-177}}, it is firm. Repeated wetting and drying, especially with heat from the sun, turns it irreversibly into ironstone hardpan or irregular aggregates. A single cycle does not. Hard plinthite looks like a mineral, but it is a product of soil formation.

soil-water-176.title: The van Genuchten model: a soil's water curve in a few numbers
soil-water-176.text: A whole {{ref:soil-water-175}} can be summed up in a few fitted numbers. The van Genuchten model is an equation that describes the shape of that curve. Its parameter α relates to the inverse of the air-entry suction, the suction at which air starts to enter the pores. The parameter n, always greater than 1, measures the pore-size distribution. Both come from field or laboratory tests, such as the instantaneous profile method, fitted by non-linear least squares. The parameterization led to a model predicting how unsaturated hydraulic conductivity varies with saturation and pressure. Alternatives include the Brooks–Corey, Broadbridge–White and Rogers–Stallybrass–Clements models.

soil-water-203.title: The darcy, a unit for how easily fluids pass
soil-water-203.text: Gravel can reach 100,000 darcys, while granite falls below 0.01 microdarcys. Sand sits near 1 darcy. The darcy is a unit of {{ref:soil-water-191}}, named after Henry Darcy, with the millidarcy as its thousandth. A medium of 1 darcy lets 1 cm³/s of a fluid with viscosity 1 cP pass through 1 cm² under a pressure gradient of 1 atm/cm. That equals 9.869233×10−13 m², usually approximated as 1 μm². It is not an SI unit, yet petroleum engineers and geologists use it widely. In hydrology, 1 darcy corresponds to a water flux of 0.831 m/day under hydrostatic pressure at 20 °C.

soil-found-071.title: The perc test: timing a hole as it drains
soil-found-071.text: Before a {{ref:soil-env-195}} or infiltration basin goes in, someone digs holes and times them. The percolation test is a field test of how fast soil absorbs water. The holes are presoaked for several hours, then filled with water to a set level, and the fall in water level is timed as it soaks away. Results in minutes per inch are matched to local health codes to size the leach field. Sandy soil generally absorbs more water than clay-rich soil or soil with a shallow water table. Not everyone trusts the test. Some jurisdictions use soil texture analysis with long-term acceptance rates instead of it or alongside it.

soil-water-244.title: Mariotte's bottle, a steady flow from a falling tank
soil-water-244.text: Mariotte's bottle delivers a constant rate of flow from a closed bottle or tank. The trick is an air inlet. It keeps the pressure at its base atmospheric, so a siphon at that depth delivers water at a constant head however far the reservoir level falls. The device is named after Edme Mariotte (1620–1684), but McCarthy first reported the design in 1934. Constant head simplifies measuring water movement in soil. The Guelph permeameter uses the principle, as do single-ring infiltrometers and the double-ring type in {{ref:soil-water-188}}. The bottle is sensitive to leaks at the air inlet and cannot be refilled while running. Electronic devices now give accurate control.

soil-water-219.title: How far apart to lay the drains
soil-water-219.text: A water table held too shallow cuts yields; one dropped too deep brings drought. A drainage equation relates the depth and spacing of parallel subsurface drains to the depth of the water table and to the depth and {{ref:soil-water-193}} of the soil. The best-known steady-state form is Hooghoudt's drain spacing equation, derived from {{ref:soil-water-201}} and introduced in the USA by van Schilfgaarde. In steady state the water table stays level and drain discharge equals the recharge rate. Given discharge, a permissible water-table depth and measured soil data, it yields the drain spacing. In one example, a seasonal average water table shallower than 70 cm depressed yield.

soil-water-220.title: Drainage research: searching for the best drain design
soil-water-220.text: Draining a field has agricultural, environmental, hydrological, engineering, economic, social and political sides, and all of them are open to research. Drainage research studies agricultural drainage systems and their effects, aiming at the design that gives optimal farm production. Water-table depth is a key factor. Drainage design controls it through {{ref:soil-water-219}}, and its link to yields is optimized to set a drainage criterion. Crop response rests on linked physical, chemical and hydrological processes. Irrigated land may need subsurface drainage to leach out salts brought in with irrigation water. Leaching models such as SaltMod help set that drainage requirement.

soil-water-190.title: The maze of large pores that steers water
soil-water-190.text: A soil's macropores do not sit alone. They link into a network, irregular in shape, size and roughness, whose geometry shapes water movement, aeration and root growth. Higher connectivity usually means higher permeability, and links to the surface and to groundwater aid infiltration and recharge. Connected is not the same as continuous. Dead-end pores block or slow water and air, while continuous pores improve aeration and give roots room. Tortuosity measures the winding: the ratio of a path's actual length to the straight distance between its two ends. The more sinuous the path, the higher the tortuosity and the resistance to flow.

soil-water-208.title: One unbroken path from soil to sky
soil-water-208.text: Water can travel from soil into a root, up a stem and out of a leaf along one connected pathway. That pathway is the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum. Water potential is very low in the air and higher inside leaves, so water diffuses out through the stomata, the pores of the leaf, as vapor. Water lost from leaf cells is replaced from the xylem, the plant's water-carrying tissue, where cohesion and tension pull more up from the roots. Soil physics, physiology and meteorology each describe their own segment in different terms. The continuum treats soil, plants, animals and air as one dynamic system, giving water in each part a {{ref:soil-water-172}}. That shared measure is the basis for modelling transport between them.

soil-water-209.title: Hydropedology, where soil science meets hydrology
soil-water-209.text: Hydrology likes to pair with the Earth's other spheres, as hydrogeology, hydroclimatology and ecohydrology show. Hydropedology is the emerging field that joins soil science and hydrology. It studies the interface between the pedosphere and the hydrosphere, the planet's water. Soil hydrology and hydropedology are both listed among the areas of practice of soil science. The biomantle shows what the field studies. Loosened by {{ref:soil-bio-047}}, it speeds downward drainage through biopores and carries throughflow downslope above dense subsoil horizons.

soil-water-246.title: Potential evapotranspiration: how much water the air demands
soil-water-246.text: Summer, clear skies, wind and nearness to the equator all raise the air's demand for water. Potential evapotranspiration is the water a crop, soil or ecosystem would evaporate and transpire if water were not limited. It reflects the energy and wind available to move water vapor, the demand side of {{ref:soil-water-161}}. Actual evapotranspiration equals it when water is ample and can never exceed it. Reference evapotranspiration, ET0, is calculated for a short-grass surface, most widely with the Penman–Monteith equation recommended by the FAO. A crop coefficient and a stress coefficient then convert it into a crop's actual evapotranspiration.

soil-water-243.title: A knowledge base that infers what was never measured
soil-water-243.text: Measure a soil's basic properties, the premise goes, and all its other physical and chemical properties follow. A soil inference system, proposed by McBratney and colleagues in 2002, builds on that premise to fill digital soil databases. It infers unknown properties with minimal uncertainty through logically linked pedotransfer functions. It computes new properties from inferred values as well as from inputs. It depends on reliable inputs, on links between basic soil data, and on quantified uncertainty. A working prototype was completed in 2007–2009 at the University of Sydney with a US partner.

soil-water-232.title: Ground that sheds rain though it counts as pervious
soil-water-232.text: Not every source of runoff is paved. Natural impervious area is land usually classed as pervious that can still yield substantial surface runoff in small and large storms. It includes open water, wetlands, rock outcrops, barren ground and compacted soils. Depending on conditions, it yields stormflow by water running over the surface, as in {{ref:soil-water-020}}, or by rain falling directly on it. Development adds more by compacting soils. Felton and Lull found in 1963 that it could cut infiltration by 80 percent. Taylor found in 1982 that construction cut infiltration rates by more than 77 percent. Its effect on runoff matters most where {{ref:soil-water-233}} is low.

soil-water-233.title: Measuring how much of a landscape is sealed
soil-water-233.text: About 76 percent of the conterminous United States has less than 1 percent impervious cover. Total impervious area is the share of an area covered by impervious surfaces, given as a fraction from zero to one or as a percentage. It is estimated in a GIS, a geographic information system, from land-cover data, land-use categories, percent developed area or population density. The US NLCD maps it in 30-metre pixels, from 0 to 100 percent. Percentage imperviousness, or PIMP, matters in drainage and can be estimated as 6.4 times the square root of the number of dwellings per hectare. PIMP is about 10% for woodland and 100% for dense commercial areas.
